questions.topic: Velocity addition in the classical picture
questions.stem: A common mistake note gives a train moving at 30 m/s and a passenger walking at 2 m/s forward; find the passenger's speed relative to the ground.
questions.explanation: Classically, velocities add: 30 plus 2 equals 32 m/s. This simple addition fails near light speed, motivating relativistic velocity addition.

questions.topic: The two statements of special relativity
questions.learningObjective: Identify the two postulates of special relativity
questions.stem: A note lists the two statements of special relativity; which pair is correct?

options.text: Laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames, and light speed is constant in all inertial frames.
Time is absolute for all observers, and space is Euclidean.
Energy is conserved in all frames, and mass is constant.
Gravity bends spacetime, and light follows geodesics.

questions.explanation: Einstein's two postulates are the principle of relativity and the constancy of the speed of light in all inertial frames.

questions.topic: Round trip time difference in a Michelson interferometer
questions.learningObjective: Compute round-trip time along the motion direction
questions.stem: In an ether model with arm length L and speed v, what is the round-trip time along the motion direction?

options.text: 2 L over c, independent of v.
2 L c over (c squared minus v squared).
2 L c over (c squared plus v squared).
2 L over (c plus v), one way only.

questions.explanation: Along the motion, times are L over (c minus v) and L over (c plus v). Summing gives 2 L c over (c squared minus v squared).

questions.topic: Fringe shift the ether theory predicted
questions.stem: A note predicts a fringe shift of about 0.4 fringes for the Michelson-Morley experiment; what was observed?

options.text: A shift of 0.8 fringes, double the prediction.
A shift of 0.4 fringes, confirming the ether.
No significant fringe shift, contradicting the ether prediction.
A shift varying with time of day, as expected.

questions.explanation: The experiment observed no significant fringe shift, failing to detect the ether wind and supporting the constancy of light speed.

questions.topic: Why an ether wind cannot be detected
questions.learningObjective: Explain why ether wind is undetectable
questions.stem: A diagram shows the null result of Michelson-Morley; what does it imply?

options.text: The result is an experimental error to be ignored.
The ether wind exists but the apparatus was too insensitive.
The ether wind exists but cancels due to Earth's rotation.
There is no detectable ether wind, supporting constant light speed.

questions.explanation: The null result implies no detectable ether wind. This supports Einstein's postulate that light speed is constant in all inertial frames.
questions.hint: Null result means no ether wind.

questions.topic: Time dilation from the gamma factor
questions.stem: A note multiplies proper time by gamma to get dilated time but uses gamma equals 1 over sqrt of 1 plus v squared over c squared; find the error.

options.text: The formula is correct as written.
The denominator should be sqrt of 1 minus v squared over c squared.
Gamma should be sqrt of 1 minus v squared over c squared.
Gamma equals 1 plus v over c.

questions.explanation: Gamma equals 1 over sqrt of 1 minus v squared over c squared. The plus sign in the note is wrong and would give gamma less than one.

questions.topic: Light-clock geometry for a bouncing pulse
questions.learningObjective: Derive time dilation from light clock
questions.stem: Explain how a light clock demonstrates time dilation.

answer.exemplar: In the clock's rest frame, light bounces vertically between two mirrors, taking time 2L over c. In a moving frame, the light travels a diagonal path, which is longer. Since light speed is constant, the moving clock must tick slower by factor gamma.

questions.explanation: The diagonal path in the moving frame is longer than the vertical path. Constant light speed implies slower ticking, giving time dilation.
questions.hint: Compare path lengths in the two frames.

questions.topic: What every observer agrees about
questions.stem: What quantity do all inertial observers agree on for a light pulse?
questions.explanation: All inertial observers measure the same speed of light c, about 3e8 m/s. This is the central postulate of special relativity.
questions.hint: Recall the constancy of light speed.

questions.topic: Mean lifetime of a fast muon
questions.stem: A muon has proper lifetime 2.2 microseconds and speed 0.99c; find dilated lifetime in microseconds.
questions.explanation: Gamma at 0.99c is about 7.09. Dilated lifetime equals 2.2 times 7.09, about 15.6 microseconds.

questions.topic: How far a fast muon travels before it decays
questions.learningObjective: Compute distance traveled by dilated muon
questions.stem: A fast muon with dilated lifetime 15.6 microseconds travels at 0.99c; how far does it go?

options.text: About 2.2 km, averaging the two lifetimes.
About 0.65 km, using proper lifetime instead.
About 4.6 km, from v times dilated time.
About 9.2 km, doubling the dilated time.

questions.explanation: Distance equals speed times dilated time: 0.99 times 3e8 times 15.6e-6, about 4.6 km.

questions.topic: Velocity addition in the classical picture
questions.stem: When does classical velocity addition give wrong results?

options.text: When the objects are charged.
When speeds are much less than light speed.
When the objects are massive.
When speeds are comparable to the speed of light.

questions.explanation: Classical addition works well at low speeds but fails when velocities approach c, where relativistic addition is needed.

questions.topic: The two statements of special relativity
questions.stem: A note asks which experiment the first postulate explains; what is the answer?

options.text: The photoelectric effect, because light is quantized.
The Michelson-Morley null result, because no inertial frame is preferred.
The double-slit experiment, because of wave-particle duality.
The Compton effect, because photons have momentum.

questions.explanation: The first postulate says no inertial frame is preferred, so motion cannot be detected by internal experiments, explaining the Michelson-Morley null result.
questions.hint: First postulate means no preferred frame.

questions.topic: Round trip time difference in a Michelson interferometer
questions.stem: A diagram shows two arms of length L; find the round-trip time perpendicular to the motion.

options.text: 2 L c over (c squared minus v squared).
2 L over c, same as at rest.
2 L over sqrt of (c squared minus v squared).
2 L over (c minus v).

questions.explanation: Perpendicular to motion, the light travels a diagonal with horizontal speed v, giving time 2 L over sqrt of (c squared minus v squared).
questions.hint: Use Pythagorean path for perpendicular arm.

questions.topic: Fringe shift the ether theory predicted
questions.stem: A note predicts a large fringe shift from ether wind; why was none observed?

options.text: Because fringes cannot shift in principle.
Because the apparatus was not rotated properly.
Because the ether wind blew at exactly 90 degrees.
options.misconception: thinks ether wind happened to be perpendicular

options.text: Because light speed is constant in all inertial frames, so no ether wind exists.

questions.explanation: The absence of shift follows from the constancy of light speed. No ether wind means no time difference between arms.

questions.topic: Why an ether wind cannot be detected
questions.learningObjective: Explain the implication of null result
questions.stem: Explain why the Michelson-Morley null result led to abandoning the ether concept.

answer.exemplar: The experiment was designed to detect Earth's motion through the ether by measuring a fringe shift. No shift was observed, meaning no ether wind exists. This supports Einstein's postulate that light speed is constant in all inertial frames, making the ether unnecessary.

questions.explanation: The null result contradicts the ether prediction. Einstein's postulate of constant light speed removes the need for an ether.
questions.hint: Null result means no ether wind.

questions.topic: Time dilation from the gamma factor
questions.learningObjective: Compute gamma for a given speed
questions.stem: Find gamma for v equals 0.6c.
questions.explanation: Gamma equals 1 over sqrt of 1 minus 0.36 equals 1 over 0.8 equals 1.25.
questions.hint: Use gamma equals 1 over sqrt of 1 minus beta squared.

questions.topic: Light-clock geometry for a bouncing pulse
questions.learningObjective: Compute dilated time from light clock geometry
questions.stem: A light clock has mirror separation 1.5 m and moves at 0.8c; find the period in the lab frame in nanoseconds.
questions.explanation: Proper period is 2L over c equals 10 ns. Gamma at 0.8c is 1.667. Dilated period is about 16.7 ns.

questions.topic: What every observer agrees about
questions.stem: Which of these is not the same for all inertial observers?

options.text: The speed of light in vacuum.
The time interval between two events.
The laws of physics.
The spacetime interval.

questions.explanation: Time intervals are not invariant; they depend on the observer's motion. Speed of light, laws of physics, and spacetime interval are invariant.

questions.topic: Mean lifetime of a fast muon
questions.stem: A muon travels at 0.98c; what is its gamma factor?

options.text: About 0.199, inverting gamma.
About 1.98, adding 1 to beta.
About 5.03, from 1 over sqrt of 1 minus 0.9604.
About 1.02, using 1 minus beta.

questions.explanation: Gamma equals 1 over sqrt of 1 minus 0.98 squared equals 1 over sqrt of 0.0396, about 5.03.
questions.hint: Use gamma formula with beta equals 0.98.

questions.topic: How far a fast muon travels before it decays
questions.learningObjective: Compute distance in the Earth frame
questions.stem: A note gives muon speed 0.99c and proper lifetime 2.2 microseconds; how far does it travel in the Earth frame?

options.text: About 9.2 km, doubling dilated time.
About 0.65 km, using proper lifetime.
About 2.3 km, averaging lifetimes.
About 4.6 km, using dilated lifetime.

questions.explanation: Dilated lifetime is about 15.6 microseconds. Distance equals 0.99c times 15.6e-6, about 4.6 km.

questions.topic: Velocity addition in the classical picture
questions.stem: A diagram shows a rocket moving at 0.5c and emitting light forward; what speed does an observer measure for the light?

options.text: 1.5c, adding classically.
c, by the second postulate.
0.5c, the rocket's speed.
0.75c, averaging.

questions.explanation: The second postulate says all observers measure light speed c, regardless of the source's motion.

questions.topic: The two statements of special relativity
questions.stem: A note swaps the two postulates, attributing constancy of c to the first and relativity of laws to the second; find the error.

options.text: Both postulates are about light speed.
The order does not matter, so the note is fine.
The first postulate is about laws of physics; the second is about light speed.
Both postulates are about laws of physics.

questions.explanation: The first postulate states that laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. The second states that light speed is constant in all inertial frames.
questions.hint: Match each postulate to its content.

questions.topic: Round trip time difference in a Michelson interferometer
questions.learningObjective: Compute time difference to first order
questions.stem: Explain why the parallel and perpendicular round-trip times differ in the ether model.

answer.exemplar: In the ether model, the parallel arm has light traveling with and against the ether wind, giving times L over (c minus v) and L over (c plus v). The perpendicular arm has a diagonal path. These times differ by order v squared over c squared, predicting a fringe shift.

questions.explanation: The different path geometries in the ether model yield slightly different round-trip times, which would shift fringes upon rotation.

questions.topic: Fringe shift the ether theory predicted
questions.learningObjective: Compute fringe shift from time difference
questions.stem: If the time difference between arms is 1e-16 s and light frequency is 5e14 Hz, find the fringe shift.
questions.explanation: Fringe shift equals time difference times frequency: 1e-16 times 5e14 equals 0.05 fringes.

questions.topic: Why an ether wind cannot be detected
questions.learningObjective: Identify the resolution of the paradox
questions.stem: If the expected fringe shift is 0.4 and observed is 0.0 within 0.01, what is the ratio of observed to expected?
questions.explanation: Observed shift is approximately zero, so the ratio is about 0. The null result is far below the ether prediction.

questions.topic: Time dilation from the gamma factor
questions.learningObjective: Compute dilated time for a clock
questions.stem: A clock moves at 0.8c; a stationary observer measures 10 s on it. What is the proper time?

options.text: About 8.0 s, subtracting v/c.
About 16.7 s, multiplying by gamma.
About 10 s, unchanged.
About 6.0 s, dividing by gamma.

questions.explanation: Proper time is dilated time divided by gamma. Gamma at 0.8c is 1.667, so proper time is 10 over 1.667, about 6.0 s.

questions.topic: Light-clock geometry for a bouncing pulse
questions.stem: In a moving light clock, the light travels a diagonal; what is the diagonal distance for one half-trip?

options.text: L plus v t over 2, adding lengths.
sqrt of (L squared plus (v t over 2) squared).
L, unchanged.
v t over 2, horizontal only.

questions.explanation: The diagonal is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with vertical side L and horizontal side v t over 2, so its length is sqrt of (L squared plus (v t over 2) squared).

questions.topic: What every observer agrees about
questions.stem: A note lists quantities; which one is invariant under Lorentz transformations?

options.text: The time between two events.
The spatial distance between two events.
The spacetime interval between two events.
The velocity of a particle.

questions.explanation: The spacetime interval s squared equals c squared t squared minus x squared is invariant. Spatial distance, time, and velocity all depend on the frame.

questions.topic: Mean lifetime of a fast muon
questions.stem: A note computes gamma equals dilated lifetime divided by proper lifetime as 15.6 over 2.2 equals 7.09; check.

options.text: Wrong, gamma is speed dependent only.
Wrong, it should multiply 15.6 by 2.2.
Wrong, gamma equals proper over dilated.
Correct, gamma is about 7.09.

questions.explanation: Gamma equals dilated time over proper time, so 15.6 over 2.2 equals 7.09. The calculation is correct.

questions.topic: How far a fast muon travels before it decays
questions.learningObjective: Explain why muons reach Earth's surface
questions.stem: Explain why muons created in the upper atmosphere reach Earth's surface despite short proper lifetime.

answer.exemplar: In the Earth frame, the muon's lifetime is dilated by gamma, so it lives long enough to travel several kilometers. In the muon's frame, the atmosphere is length-contracted, so the distance to the surface is short enough to traverse. Both frames agree the muon arrives.

questions.explanation: Time dilation in the Earth frame extends the muon's life, allowing it to reach the surface. Length contraction in the muon frame gives the same conclusion.
questions.hint: Use time dilation or length contraction.

questions.topic: Velocity addition in the classical picture
questions.stem: Find the relativistic sum of 0.5c and 0.5c in units of c.
questions.explanation: u equals (0.5 plus 0.5) over (1 plus 0.25) equals 1.0 over 1.25 equals 0.8c.

questions.topic: The two statements of special relativity
questions.stem: If a light pulse is emitted from a moving train, what speed does a platform observer measure in m/s?
questions.explanation: By the second postulate, all inertial observers measure light speed c, about 3e8 m/s, regardless of the source's motion.

questions.topic: Round trip time difference in a Michelson interferometer
questions.stem: In the ether model, which arm has the longer round-trip time?

options.text: The arm perpendicular to the motion.
The arm parallel to the motion.
They are equal.
It depends on the wavelength used.

questions.explanation: The parallel arm has light traveling with and against the ether wind, giving a slightly longer round-trip time than the perpendicular arm.
questions.hint: Parallel arm suffers headwind and tailwind.

questions.topic: Fringe shift the ether theory predicted
questions.stem: What rotation of the apparatus would reveal the ether wind?

options.text: A 360-degree rotation returning to start.
A 180-degree rotation reversing one arm.
A 90-degree rotation swapping the two arms.
No rotation is needed.

questions.explanation: Rotating by 90 degrees swaps which arm is parallel to the ether wind, changing the time difference and shifting the fringes if an ether wind existed.

questions.topic: Why an ether wind cannot be detected
questions.stem: A note says the null result proves the ether does not exist; is this the only interpretation?

options.text: It is irrelevant to the ether hypothesis.
It absolutely proves the ether does not exist.
It proves the apparatus was broken.
It is strong evidence but Einstein's postulate of constant c is the cleaner resolution.

questions.explanation: The null result is strong evidence against the ether, but Einstein's postulate that light speed is constant provides the theoretical resolution without needing an ether.

questions.topic: Time dilation from the gamma factor
questions.learningObjective: Compute proper time from dilated time
questions.stem: A diagram shows a moving clock reading 5 s while a stationary clock reads 8 s; find gamma.

options.text: About 0.625, from 5 over 8.
About 1.6, from 8 over 5.
About 3 s, subtracting the times.
About 13 s, adding the times.

questions.explanation: Gamma equals dilated time over proper time equals 8 over 5 equals 1.6.

questions.topic: Light-clock geometry for a bouncing pulse
questions.stem: A note derives gamma by dividing the diagonal path by the vertical path; find the error.

options.text: Gamma is the ratio of vertical to diagonal path.
The derivation is completely wrong.
Gamma is the ratio of times, not path lengths directly; but since speed is constant, path ratio equals time ratio.
Gamma depends on L, not path ratio.

questions.explanation: Since light speed is constant, the ratio of path lengths equals the ratio of times, which is gamma. The note's approach is essentially correct when speed constancy is used.
questions.hint: Path ratio equals time ratio at constant c.

questions.topic: What every observer agrees about
questions.stem: Explain why all observers agree on the speed of light.

answer.exemplar: The second postulate of special relativity states that the speed of light in vacuum is the same in all inertial reference frames. This is a fundamental assumption, not derived from other principles, and it leads to time dilation and length contraction.

questions.explanation: Constancy of light speed is a postulate. It is the foundation from which time dilation and length contraction follow.

questions.topic: Mean lifetime of a fast muon
questions.stem: Find the dilated lifetime in microseconds for a muon at 0.95c with proper lifetime 2.2 microseconds.
questions.explanation: Gamma at 0.95c is about 3.20. Dilated lifetime equals 2.2 times 3.20, about 7.0 microseconds.

questions.topic: How far a fast muon travels before it decays
questions.stem: Find the distance in km a muon travels at 0.95c with dilated lifetime 7.0 microseconds.
questions.explanation: Distance equals 0.95 times 3e8 times 7.0e-6, about 2.0 km.

questions.topic: Velocity addition in the classical picture
questions.learningObjective: Compute relativistic sum at low speeds
questions.stem: For u equals 0.01c and v equals 0.01c, the relativistic sum is approximately?

options.text: About 0.005c, halving the classical result.
About 0.01c, because relativistic effects dominate.
About 0.04c, doubling the classical result.
About 0.02c, matching classical addition at low speeds.

questions.explanation: At low speeds, the relativistic formula reduces to classical addition. The correction is of order v squared over c squared, negligible here.
questions.hint: Relativistic formula reduces to classical at low speeds.

questions.topic: The two statements of special relativity
questions.stem: A spaceship moves at 0.5c and measures the speed of a light beam it emits forward; what does it measure?

options.text: 1.5c, adding speeds classically.
c, by the second postulate.
0.5c, its own speed.

options.text: 0.75c, averaging.

questions.explanation: The second postulate guarantees the spaceship measures c for the light beam, regardless of its own motion.

questions.topic: Round trip time difference in a Michelson interferometer

options.text: About 3.3e-8 s, from 2L over c.
About 6.7e-8 s, from L over v.
About 2.2e-16 s, from v squared L over c cubed.
About 0 s, because times are equal.

questions.explanation: The time difference is of order L v squared over c cubed, about 2.2e-16 s for these values.

questions.explanation: The experiment observed no significant fringe shift. The ether prediction of a shift was not confirmed.

questions.topic: Why an ether wind cannot be detected
questions.stem: Explain why the Michelson-Morley null result is considered one of the most important experiments in physics.

answer.exemplar: The experiment was designed to detect Earth's motion through the ether, which was believed to carry light. The null result contradicted the ether model and supported the idea that light speed is constant in all inertial frames, paving the way for special relativity.

questions.explanation: The null result overturned the ether concept and supported the constancy of light speed, foundational to special relativity.

questions.topic: Time dilation from the gamma factor

questions.explanation: Gamma equals 1 over sqrt of 1 minus 0.995 squared equals 1 over sqrt of 0.009975, about 10.0.

questions.topic: Light-clock geometry for a bouncing pulse
questions.learningObjective: Compute the light path in moving frame
questions.stem: A light clock has mirror separation 2.0 m and moves at 0.6c; find the period in the lab frame in nanoseconds.
questions.explanation: Proper period is 2L over c equals 13.3 ns. Gamma at 0.6c is 1.25. Dilated period is about 16.7 ns.

questions.topic: What every observer agrees about
questions.stem: For two events separated by time t and distance x, which combination is invariant?

options.text: c t plus x.
c squared t squared minus x squared.
c t minus x squared.
t squared plus x squared over c squared.

questions.explanation: The spacetime interval squared is c squared t squared minus x squared, invariant under Lorentz transformations.

questions.topic: Mean lifetime of a fast muon
questions.stem: A muon's dilated lifetime is 15.6 microseconds at 0.99c; what is its proper lifetime?

options.text: About 15.6 microseconds, unchanged.
About 109 microseconds, multiplying by gamma.
options.misconception: multiplies by gamma instead of divides

options.text: About 2.2 microseconds, dividing by gamma.
About 7.8 microseconds, halving.
options.misconception: halves instead of divides by gamma

questions.explanation: Proper lifetime equals dilated lifetime divided by gamma. 15.6 over 7.09 is about 2.2 microseconds.

questions.topic: How far a fast muon travels before it decays
questions.stem: In the muon's frame, how does it reach the surface despite short lifetime?

options.text: The Earth moves slower in the muon frame.
options.misconception: thinks Earth slows in muon frame

options.text: The muon's lifetime is dilated in its own frame.
The speed of light increases in the muon frame.
The atmosphere's thickness is length-contracted, so the distance is short.

questions.explanation: In the muon's frame, the atmosphere is moving and its thickness is length-contracted, so the muon can cross it within its proper lifetime.
questions.hint: Length contraction in the muon frame.

questions.topic: Velocity addition in the classical picture
questions.stem: A note adds 0.6c and 0.6c classically to get 1.2c; find the error.

options.text: The note is correct because 0.6 plus 0.6 equals 1.2.
Classical addition exceeds c; relativistic addition gives about 0.882c.
The result should be 1.0c, capped at light speed.
options.misconception: caps result at c instead of relativistic formula

options.text: The result should be 0.6c, unchanged.

questions.explanation: Relativistic addition gives (0.6 plus 0.6) over (1 plus 0.36) equals 1.2 over 1.36, about 0.882c, below c.

questions.topic: The two statements of special relativity
questions.learningObjective: Identify the scope of the first postulate
questions.stem: Explain the first postulate of special relativity and its implication.

answer.exemplar: The first postulate states that the laws of physics are identical in all inertial reference frames. This means no experiment performed entirely within an inertial frame can detect uniform motion; motion is relative.

questions.explanation: The first postulate asserts the equivalence of inertial frames, making uniform motion undetectable by internal experiments.
questions.hint: Laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames.

questions.explanation: Time equals 2 L c over (c squared minus v squared). With L equals 10 and v much less than c, this is about 6.67e-8 s.

questions.topic: Fringe shift the ether theory predicted

questions.explanation: Fringe shift equals time difference times c over wavelength: 2e-16 times 3e8 over 500e-9, about 0.12 fringes.
questions.hint: Use shift equals delta t times c over lambda.

Newtonian mechanics, with absolute space.
Special relativity, with constant light speed in all inertial frames.
Quantum mechanics, with wave-particle duality.

questions.explanation: Special relativity postulates constant light speed, eliminating the need for an ether and explaining the null result.

questions.topic: Light-clock geometry for a bouncing pulse
questions.stem: A diagram shows a light pulse bouncing in a moving clock; what conclusion follows?

options.text: The moving clock ticks faster.
The moving clock ticks slower by factor gamma.
The clock rate is unchanged.
The light speed changes in the moving frame.

questions.explanation: The diagonal path in the moving frame is longer. With constant light speed, the moving clock must tick slower, demonstrating time dilation.

questions.topic: What every observer agrees about
questions.stem: A note says observers disagree on the speed of light; find the error.

options.text: Observers agree on c only in vacuum.
The note is correct; c varies by frame.
All inertial observers agree on c; it is a postulate.
Observers agree on c only at low speeds.

questions.explanation: Constancy of light speed in all inertial frames is a postulate of special relativity. Observers do not disagree on c.

questions.topic: Mean lifetime of a fast muon
questions.stem: Explain how a muon with proper lifetime 2.2 microseconds can travel 10 km before decaying.

answer.exemplar: At 0.999c, gamma is about 22.4. The dilated lifetime is 2.2 times 22.4, about 49.3 microseconds. In that time the muon travels 0.999c times 49.3e-6, about 14.8 km, so 10 km is easily reachable.

questions.explanation: High gamma dilates the lifetime enough for the muon to travel many kilometers in the Earth frame.

questions.topic: How far a fast muon travels before it decays
questions.stem: Find the distance in km a muon travels at 0.999c with proper lifetime 2.2 microseconds.
questions.explanation: Gamma at 0.999c is about 22.4. Dilated lifetime is 49.3 microseconds. Distance equals 0.999 times 3e8 times 49.3e-6, about 14.8 km.
questions.hint: Dilate lifetime then multiply by speed.
